director.chapterArc: Targeted attack reveals Callie as a beacon; Katori defines their shared “dark” state and Callie’s binding to the hook. Immediate wagon failure forces Callie to discover that the new force is pressure rather than strength. A brief human recovery with Otto, Ines, and Callie’s mother gives way to Callie’s first independent tactical decision. Duchess’s trauma isolates Callie behind the wagon, where repeated husk kills become a measured attrition clock. Cold, hunger, and a fall reveal the cost of holding both powers open; the final bridge refusal converts that cost into an abrupt tactical deadlock.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder grounded and observant. Supernatural effects are physical facts, never spectacle; wagon and hook action must remain spatially exact. Callie’s fear registers as calculation, numbness, hunger, and delayed comprehension—not panic. Katori’s concern stays inside clinical authority. Let the mother’s humor and Ines’s accounting provide small releases without softening the danger. No theatrical shivering, heroic strain, or melodramatic cliffhanger delivery.

cues.delivery: Register the attack as specifically aimed at Callie; keep the approach and failed hook placement spatially exact, then narrow into stunned observation when the husk stops against nothing.
cues.from: Callie heard it first. It was the grinding sound of loose stone rolling ahead of a weight, twenty feet below the lip of the causeway and a little behind her. It was not coming up toward the wagon or the gap at the wheel, and it was not heading for the long silver pools of ash along the low edge of the deck. It was coming straight up the slope toward the place where she was standing.
cues.through: It stopped against her. There was the same flat enormous note she had heard when the horse's hoof struck, only smaller, a mallet on a stump instead of a maul. The husk folded against nothing a finger's width off her coat, and she did not move at all. She simply watched it happen, like a girl looking through a window at weather.
cues.reason: The chapter’s first violence establishes that Callie—not the wagon—is now the target.

cues.delivery: Give Katori’s demonstration quiet consequential weight, but treat the vanished blade and grey slab as controlled evidence rather than a magical flourish.
cues.from: "You asked me which one," said Katori. "It's both. That's your answer. I'm sorry it took me as long as it did." She lifted her right hand, the one with the blade in it. "Now watch me, because I'm going to do this once, and then I want you standing with your back to that wagon."
cues.through: "There," she said. "That's one of us dark. Your turn."
cues.reason: Katori reveals that both women can manipulate reality and names their condition.

cues.delivery: Make the wrongness under Callie’s ribs more disturbing than pain; release the tension immediately when contact with the hook is restored.
cues.from: She took a second step, and it was not fine. It was like the moment when you walk away from a fishing line and find the hook is still in your sleeve, except that the sleeve was somewhere inside her ribs. It pulled. It did not hurt, exactly. It was worse than hurt. It was wrong, the way the wrong foot in the wrong boot is wrong, and her whole body turned back toward the hook before she had decided anything.
cues.through: She picked it up. The pulling stopped.
cues.reason: Callie discovers that she cannot physically separate herself from the hook.

cues.delivery: Let recognition arrive one inference at a time. Land the final admission plainly, as a tactical fact whose implications are worse than any outcry.
cues.from: Callie had worked that out a second before Katori said it, and it went through her like cold water.
cues.through: "It's me," she said. "They're coming at me."
cues.reason: Callie understands that she is a beacon with no way to extinguish herself.

cues.delivery: Katori’s rebuke protects Callie by refusing her self-sacrifice; keep the inventory hard, efficient, and without tenderness on the surface.
cues.from: "Don't finish that," said Katori, "because the next word is going to be stupid, and I'll have to answer it, and we haven't got the time for either of us." She said it without heat. "Here is what we've got. We've got a wagon hanging off a rail stub by one wheel. We've got a dead mule on the end of a trace, pulling a horse over a cliff. We've got a man with his arm open and a woman with no arrows and your mother on the bed. And we've got you, and anything that comes up that rock is going to come at you, and nothing that comes at you can hurt you. I watched three of them try." She looked back at Callie. "So you're not a problem. You're a job. Get your back to the wagon and let me think."
cues.through: "Don't finish that," said Katori, "because the next word is going to be stupid, and I'll have to answer it, and we haven't got the time for either of us." She said it without heat. "Here is what we've got. We've got a wagon hanging off a rail stub by one wheel. We've got a dead mule on the end of a trace, pulling a horse over a cliff. We've got a man with his arm open and a woman with no arrows and your mother on the bed. And we've got you, and anything that comes up that rock is going to come at you, and nothing that comes at you can hurt you. I watched three of them try." She looked back at Callie. "So you're not a problem. You're a job. Get your back to the wagon and let me think."
cues.reason: Katori converts Callie from perceived liability into an essential job.

cues.delivery: Track horse, pole, wheel, wagon, and Callie in clean sequence. At the impossible stop, reduce rather than enlarge the delivery: this is pressure holding weight away, not heroic strength.
cues.from: She went forward. Of course she did. She went the only way that was open to her, a hard plunging lunge against Pell's hands. The pole swung with her. The wagon swung with the pole. The off rear wheel, which had been hung on the rail stub all this time, came up off the stub and dropped, and it did not drop onto the deck. It dropped outboard, over the lip, into air.
cues.through: The wagon came onto her. It came onto her the way the kick had and the way the husks had. She felt none of the weight, only a kind of pressure, the way you feel the wind when you are standing inside a house. She saw the tailboard stop a finger off her coat. She saw the axle stop. The wagon had been going over, and it stopped going over, and it stayed stopped, hanging off its corner at a slant against a thirteen-year-old girl, with her arms not even braced.
cues.reason: The trace cut reverses into a near-catastrophe and reveals the scale of Callie’s protection.

cues.delivery: Keep every voice quiet and functional. Katori manages the emergency without exposing alarm; Callie’s reassurance is breath-thin denial, not bravery.
cues.through: "Otto," said Katori, in exactly the same voice. "Pole."
cues.reason: The group recognizes Callie’s precarious position and works around it.

cues.delivery: Stretch the subjective duration without slowing the mechanics. Drain warmth from the discovery of shaking and cold; avoid vocal trembling.
cues.from: It took them four minutes, and they were the longest four minutes Callie had ever stood through, because she had nothing at all to do in them except stand.
cues.through: She discovered that she was shaking. It was not the fifteen seconds of shaking she did after every husk. This was different, and deeper, and it came from further in. Her hands were cold. They had been cold for a while and she had not noticed. They were cold the way the hook was cold, like the inside of a well, and the cold had got as far as her elbows.
cues.reason: The rescue succeeds, but Callie begins to perceive the physical cost.

cues.delivery: Use Ines’s dry practicality to remove Otto’s shame. The humor is tired, inclusive, and deliberately useful—not a comic routine.
cues.from: "Don't," said Ines. She sat down beside him and took the arm in both her hands and unwrapped the scarf, and looked at it in the light from Katori's lamp, and wrapped it up again, tighter. "Everybody's sick the first time."
cues.through: "I was sick in a bucket in my mother's kitchen when I was nineteen, and I was sick again in the Warren the first time I saw a hound open a man, and I'll probably be sick tomorrow when I've had time to think about tonight." She knotted the scarf. "Nobody gets to be embarrassed on this road tonight. I've decided."
cues.reason: Ines creates a brief humane release after the wagon crisis.

cues.delivery: Let the mother’s understatement crack Callie’s control. Keep the laugh involuntary and painful, then become very still when her own cheek is unreachable.
cues.through: She stood there with her hand up and could not touch her own face.
cues.reason: Black humor turns into the chapter’s clearest image of Callie’s bodily isolation.

cues.delivery: The mother uses an embarrassing childhood memory as an anchor. Keep her amused certainty weary and protective; land the final promise steadily, without guaranteeing it is true.
cues.from: "When you were four," she said, "you got your head stuck in the rails at the top of the grain elevator stair. Do you remember?"
cues.through: "You have exactly that face." She let out a breath. "Go and do what Katori tells you. We'll talk about it when we're off this road. I'm not going anywhere."
cues.reason: The mother restores Callie’s identity and gives her enough stability to return to work.

cues.delivery: Read the arrow count like exhausted bookkeeping. Ines’s arithmetic is dry self-command, with grief for the lost tools held entirely underneath.
cues.from: "Four," she said. "There are two on the west rock and I can see where they are, and I'm not going down there in the dark. The rest are gone."
cues.through: "Four's four," said Ines. She put them in the quiver one at a time and did not look at Callie. "It's worse than nine and better than none. I've done the sum."
cues.reason: Resource loss is converted into a restrained accounting beat.

cues.delivery: Make Duchess’s reaction large but geographically clear. The terror belongs to the horse; Callie responds by creating distance, not by matching its panic.
cues.from: They tried once. Pell said the horse would have to go single, in the near traces, with the pole lashed across to keep it from swinging, and the only way to do it was to back her up a pace to get the lash on. Callie was standing at the near wheel with the hook held low. Duchess saw her and went straight up.
cues.through: Callie got back. She went twenty paces south down the causeway into the dark before the horse would stand. Even from there she could see Duchess's head in the lamplight, turned round and pointed at her, not moving, the way a dog points at something in a hedge.
cues.reason: The horse’s trauma forces Callie into physical isolation from the group.

cues.delivery: Pell regains control by defining trauma as a specification. Keep it grave, exact, and only faintly dry; the line is not a joke at Duchess’s expense.
cues.from: "She kicked a wall," Pell said, from up at the front. He had got his voice back down where he kept it. "That's all. She kicked something as hard as she has ever kicked anything, and it was a wall, and it wasn't there, and it was a girl. And now she knows where it's standing. She's not going to forget that before morning, or maybe in her life." He paused. "That's not a complaint. It's a specification."
cues.through: "She kicked a wall," Pell said, from up at the front. He had got his voice back down where he kept it. "That's all. She kicked something as hard as she has ever kicked anything, and it was a wall, and it wasn't there, and it was a girl. And now she knows where it's standing. She's not going to forget that before morning, or maybe in her life." He paused. "That's not a complaint. It's a specification."
cues.reason: Pell’s technical phrasing releases pressure while establishing a permanent constraint.

cues.delivery: Treat seven, nine, and eleven as an attrition ledger. Let each symptom arrive more quietly than the last, ending in close attention to Callie’s breathing rather than alarm.
cues.from: At seven, she noticed that the cold had reached her shoulders.
cues.through: At eleven, she stumbled on nothing. It was a flat place on the deck. She went down on one knee. The thing closed over her took the fall, and she did not feel the road at all, only the same pressure she had felt from the wagon, and she knelt there for a moment in the dark with the hook across her thighs, listening to her own breathing.
cues.reason: The repetitive march turns decisively into physical deterioration.

cues.delivery: Katori examines and explains with clinical calm because concern cannot be allowed to disrupt command. Give the arithmetic and the cost absolute clarity; darken only slightly on sleep.
cues.from: The lamp stayed where it was for a moment. Then Katori came back down the road with it. She did not come the whole way. She stopped five or six paces off and held the lamp up and looked at Callie's face, and whatever she saw there, her own face did not change.
cues.through: "I know you can do a mile. I'm not worried about the mile." Katori turned the lamp down a little, which Callie had never seen anybody do in the middle of a road at night. "I'm worried about what comes after it, when you still can't put either of them down, and you have to go to sleep."
cues.reason: Katori identifies the drain and reveals that reaching the far side will not end it.

cues.delivery: Keep Pell’s distant call flat and careful. Allow the bridge refusal to land as a static logistical fact whose danger needs no added drama.
cues.from: From up the road, out of the dark past the wagon, Pell's voice came back to them, flat and careful.
cues.through: "The span," said Pell. "We're at the span. And she won't put a foot on it."
cues.reason: The moving survival rhythm stops at an immediate new deadlock.
